concepts.name: Bahmani Architectural Style: Origins and Synthesis
key_dimensions: Blend of Persian, Turkish, and local Deccan (Hindu-Chalukyan) traditions
Distinction from Delhi Sultanate architectural canon — why Deccan diverged
Role of foreign craftsmen and travellers (Ibn Battuta, Mahmud Gawan's connections) in stylistic import
UPSC trap: Bahmani style is NOT a direct derivative of Tughlaq architecture despite political lineage

concepts.name: Gulbarga Fort and Jama Masjid: Earliest Bahmani Monuments
key_dimensions: Gulbarga as the first Bahmani capital and its architectural significance
Jama Masjid, Gulbarga — unique feature: entire courtyard covered with arcaded roof (no open courtyard), modeled on Córdoba mosque — a UPSC trap point
Spanish/Moorish influence versus Persian influence debate
Comparison with later Bahmani mosques to trace stylistic evolution

concepts.name: Bidar as the Shifted Capital: Architectural Transition
key_dimensions: Shift of capital from Gulbarga to Bidar under Ahmad Shah I (1430s) and its architectural implications
Bidar Fort complex — Persian influence peaks, use of coloured tiles (Kashi work)
Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan: landmark Persian-influenced structure, its current ruined state
Distinction between Gulbarga-phase and Bidar-phase Bahmani architecture for exam comparisons

concepts.name: Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan, Bidar
key_dimensions: Architectural features: three-storeyed structure, minarets, Persian-style tile mosaic facade
Educational and architectural dual significance — one of few surviving madrasas of medieval India
Partial destruction by gunpowder explosion and current status as a protected monument
UPSC trap: Often confused with similar Persian-style structures; it is explicitly Persian (not Indo-Saracenic)

concepts.name: Bahmani Tombs at Ashtur (Near Bidar)
key_dimensions: Series of royal Bahmani tombs — large bulbous domes as a defining Deccan feature
Contrast with Delhi Sultanate tombs (Lodi garden tombs) in dome style and ornamentation
Use of stucco decoration and Persian calligraphy in interiors
UPSC angle: Bulbous/swelling dome as a marker to distinguish Deccan tombs from North Indian ones

concepts.name: Adil Shahi Architecture of Bijapur: Defining Features
key_dimensions: Bijapur (Adil Shahi Sultanate) as the most architecturally prolific of the five Deccan Sultanates
Stylistic hallmarks: large bulbous domes, flat-roofed mosques, profuse ornamentation, bracketed cornices
Persian + Hindu + local synthesis more pronounced than in Bahmani phase
Gol Gumbaz and Ibrahim Rauza as the two poles of Adil Shahi architecture — contrasting philosophies

concepts.name: Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: Engineering and Architectural Significance
key_dimensions: Tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah — second largest dome in the world (after St. Peter's Basilica, Rome) — a key UPSC fact
Whispering gallery: acoustic feature created by the circular balcony inside the dome
Pendentives and squinches used to transition from square base to circular dome — structural innovation
UPSC trap: Gol Gumbaz dome is larger than the Pantheon dome — comparative fact frequently tested

concepts.name: Ibrahim Rauza, Bijapur: The 'Poem in Stone'
key_dimensions: Tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II — considered the most refined and ornate Adil Shahi monument
Described as inspiration for the Taj Mahal by some historians — a contested but frequently cited claim
Features: slender minarets, delicate stone tracery (jali work), balanced composition of tomb + mosque
Contrast with Gol Gumbaz: Ibrahim Rauza prioritizes elegance; Gol Gumbaz prioritizes scale

concepts.name: Deccan Dome Typology: Bulbous vs. Persian vs. Mughal Domes
key_dimensions: Deccan bulbous dome: sits directly on the drum, broader at base, distinct from Mughal double dome
Persian influence: use of coloured tile work (Kashi/Chini kari) on dome exteriors in Bidar phase
Mughal dome comparison: Mughal domes are more elevated, use double-shell construction — UPSC trap area
Qutb Shahi domes (Golconda) as a sub-variant: even more pronounced bulge, distinctive green/turquoise tiles

concepts.name: Qutb Shahi Architecture of Golconda and Hyderabad
key_dimensions: Qutb Shahi tombs near Golconda Fort: one of the largest necropolis complexes in India
Architectural features: pointed arches, bulging domes on high drums, intricate stucco, Persian inscriptions
Charminar (1591): built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah — mosque + gateway hybrid, symbol of Hyderabad
UPSC trap: Charminar was built to commemorate the end of a plague, not as a victory monument

concepts.name: Charminar: Symbolism, Function, and Architecture
key_dimensions: Four minarets = four Khalifas of Islam (symbolic interpretation) vs. functional role as city gateway + mosque
Structural features: four grand arches, upper-floor mosque, stucco ornamentation, minarets with balconies
Urban planning significance: Charminar as the centre of the newly founded city of Hyderabad
UPSC comparison trap: Charminar is often juxtaposed with Char Minar of other regions — it is unique in mosque-gateway fusion

concepts.name: Imad Shahi and Berar Architecture: The Lesser-Known Sultanate
key_dimensions: Imad Shahi sultanate (Berar) — least architecturally documented of the five Deccan Sultanates
Gawilgarh and Narnala forts as key surviving structures — military rather than religious architecture
Absorbed into Ahmadnagar Sultanate (1574) — architectural tradition cut short
UPSC relevance: Negative knowledge — knowing which sultanate left minimal architectural legacy

concepts.name: Nizam Shahi Architecture of Ahmadnagar
key_dimensions: Farah Bagh and Bagh-i-Nizam: Persian-style garden complexes showing Timurid influence
Tomb of Ahmad Nizam Shah and the Damri Mosque as foundational Nizam Shahi monuments
Ahmadnagar Fort: significant military architecture, site of Chand Bibi's defence
Stylistic position between Bahmani legacy and Adil Shahi/Qutb Shahi refinement

concepts.name: Barid Shahi Architecture of Bidar: Continuity and Innovation
key_dimensions: Barid Shahi tombs in Bidar — built after Bahmani collapse, retain tile-mosaic tradition
Ali Barid's tomb: notable for being open-sided (no walls), unique in Indian funerary architecture
Continuation of Kashi tile work from Bahmani period — stylistic continuity as an exam angle
UPSC trap: Bidar has monuments of BOTH Bahmani AND Barid Shahi periods — must distinguish them

concepts.name: Persian Influence in Deccan Architecture: Specific Markers
key_dimensions: Kashi/tile work (blue, turquoise, green glazed tiles) on facades and domes — Bidar and Golconda specific
Pointed Persian arches vs. the more rounded arches of North India
Use of calligraphy (Naskh and Nasta'liq scripts) as decorative element — more elaborate than Delhi tradition
Char bagh garden layouts in Deccan sultans' palaces — Persian paradise garden concept

concepts.name: Hindu-Deccani Synthesis in Architecture: Local Assimilation
key_dimensions: Incorporation of Chalukyan and Kakatiya decorative motifs (lotus, kirtimukha, bracket figures) in Deccan sultanate buildings
Use of local basalt stone alongside imported Persian design vocabulary
Flat-roofed prayer halls in some Deccan mosques — derived from local Hindu/Jain temple traditions
UPSC trap: This synthesis is MORE pronounced in Deccan than in Delhi Sultanate architecture — a comparative distinction

concepts.name: Military Architecture of the Deccan Sultanates
key_dimensions: Golconda Fort: concentric fortification, acoustic signalling system, water supply engineering — frequently tested
Daulatabad (Devagiri) Fort: earlier Yadava origin, adapted by Bahmani and later Mughals — multilayered history
Bidar Fort: use of coloured tilework even in military structures — unique crossover of decorative and defensive
UPSC angle: Golconda Fort's acoustics (clapping at the entrance heard at the top) as a specific factual trap

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: Deccan Sultanate vs. Mughal Architecture
key_dimensions: Dome construction: Deccan bulbous single-shell dome vs. Mughal elevated double-shell dome
Ornamentation: Deccan uses tile mosaic and stucco; Mughals use pietra dura (inlay with precious stones)
Minaret style: Deccan minarets are shorter, bulkier; Mughal minarets are tall, slender, detached
UPSC trap: Ibrahim Rauza's influence on Taj Mahal — acknowledging Deccan precedent in Mughal architecture

concepts.name: Garden Tombs and Funerary Architecture in the Deccan
key_dimensions: Concept of the garden tomb (rauza) as distinct from the standalone tomb platform
Ibrahim Rauza as the finest example — mosque and tomb in a shared walled garden
Qutb Shahi tombs complex: multiple tombs in a garden setting, a necropolis model
UPSC angle: How Deccan garden tombs predate and possibly influence the Mughal garden tomb tradition (Humayun's Tomb → Taj)

concepts.name: Bijapur Mosque Architecture: Evolution from Bahmani to Adil Shahi
key_dimensions: Jama Masjid, Bijapur: large hypostyle hall, ornate mihrab, no fully enclosed courtyard — contrast with Gulbarga
Mihrab decoration: use of calligraphy and geometric patterns, absence of figurative art (Islamic orthodoxy)
Makka Masjid, Hyderabad (Qutb Shahi): one of the largest mosques in India, granite construction, 15 arches facade
UPSC trap: Makka Masjid name origin — stones from Mecca embedded in the central arch, NOT because it faces Mecca (it does face Mecca, but the name has a different reason)
